Vignette: Margaret

Margaret is a 63-year-old married woman of European descent who works as a sculptor from a studio attached to her home in a rural setting. She has spent most of her adult life working with her hands - shaping stone and clay into forms she describes as "things that were always there, waiting to be found." For decades, her work gave her a sense of control and quiet mastery over the physical world. That sense of safety collapsed entirely eighteen months ago, when she was raped by a man she knew - a gallery associate who had come to her studio to discuss an upcoming exhibition. Her husband was away for the weekend. No one else was nearby.

In the immediate aftermath, Margaret did not call the police. She tells it the way many survivors do - she cleaned herself up, she made tea, she sat at the kitchen table for a very long time not knowing what she was sitting with. She told her husband several days later. She describes his response as loving but helpless, and she found herself consoling him, setting her own experience aside in a way that has become a pattern she is only now beginning to recognize.

The studio, once her sanctuary, became something else entirely. The assault happened there, on the concrete floor near the workbench where she still keeps her chisels and rasps. For the first two months she did not enter it at all. When she finally tried to return to work, the smell of stone dust - a smell she had always loved - triggered an immediate and overwhelming physical response: her heart raced, her vision narrowed, and she found herself back on that floor, not remembering it but reliving it, with a vividness that left her shaking and nauseated. She has since moved much of her work to a rented space in a nearby town, but even there, certain angles of afternoon light, the sound of a door opening unexpectedly, or the particular weight of a man's footstep in the hallway can send her back.

Sleep has become a negotiation with dread. She goes to bed late, often sitting up reading until her husband falls asleep, and when she does sleep she frequently wakes in the early hours, heart pounding, with fragments of the assault moving through her mind like something she cannot put down. She has stopped dreaming about anything else. During the day she moves through stretches of numbness that she describes as "being made of the same material as my sculptures - present but not alive." She has withdrawn from friends and from the small professional community she once enjoyed, finding social gatherings effortful in a way that feels almost physical, as though she is wearing something heavy.

There is a particular quality of shame that runs beneath everything Margaret says. She returns often to the fact that she knew him, that she had poured wine, that she had been, in her words, "warm and professional and completely unaware." She has constructed an elaborate internal argument about her own culpability that she presents with the precision of someone who has rehearsed it many times and found it, each time, convincing. She is angry - she will say that clearly - but the anger turns inward with a speed that catches her off guard.

Her sculpting, when she manages it, has changed. She is working almost exclusively in broken forms now - pieces that are deliberately fractured, surfaces left rough where she once would have refined them. She says she doesn't know if this is art or just evidence. She brings photographs of the work to sessions and sets them on the table between herself and the therapist without explanation, as though they say something she has not yet found words for. In many ways, they do.

Margaret presents as a woman of considerable intelligence and resilience who is struggling, profoundly, to integrate an experience that has altered her relationship to her body, her work, her home, and her own history. She is, as she puts it, "still here - but not where I was."
